412.t: Feather and Ulanov attack Hodes and the moldy figs
412.s: Hodes says Leonard Feather and Barry Ulanov made him a focal point of attacks on traditional jazz. Pee Wee Russell and Louis Armstrong also took shots.
412.ch: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
412.q: Feather and Barry Ulanov, who was fixing Leonard's coattails, so to speak, and then a few more that followed in their footsteps because they seemed like winners. And this is what--

412.t: Who started the jazz war, and the Irish judge
412.s: Hodes and DeMichael agree the writers started the bitterness. Feather's lawsuit against Hodes's friend was dismissed by an Irish judge.
412.ch: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
412.q: It wasn't -- it was the writer. Feather was the first one that wrote anything. Now, why he started it is something else. Or whether he had cause.

412.t: Hodes's diary and writing the book about the jazz war
412.s: They discuss Hodes's diary from this period and what it feels like to be attacked by one writer in every review.
412.ch: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
412.q: I've still got a diary. And I can't find all the screaming words, but I found one piece of paper where I says, what is he, God? I have decreed what jazz is and what isn't.

412.t: The friendly Look review of Selections from the Gutter
412.s: Hodes says Feather wrote a complimentary Look review of the Gutter record, probably arranged by Milt Gabler before the argument.
412.ch: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
412.q: But you don't know the worst part about it. Let me tell you the worst part, which will go in the book. Is, I got a writeup in Look magazine, and I still have that, in which he reviewed Selections From the Gutter. And it was a very complimentary thing.

412.t: Polls, Who's Who and the power of the press
412.s: Hodes says his name never appeared in the polls or in Who's Who for years. He recounts the Disneyland booking lost after a review and a bad DownBeat review.
412.ch: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
412.q: Well, I just name one. Don't you think it hurt Edmund Hall? Sure, Louis gave him some work and all that, but don't you think it hurts -- okay, take me. I look on the polls and I don't see my name on there, time after time after time. It never appears. And for the longest time, I wasn't even in the…

412.t: Feather as a writer and the planned book chapter
412.s: Hodes calls Feather a good craftsman but says his motives are suspect. He wants the jazz war included in the book.
412.ch: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
412.q: Who else put out a Who's Who on jazz? Year after year, and things like that. To a certain extent, a lot of that is important, because if he doesn't hate you, you might get a lot of factual stuff there. At least, I don't know who else is doing it.

412.s: Hodes says Feather would want to forget this period. DeMichael says Feather mellowed after a serious accident.
412.ch: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
412.q: But I used to have an agent that loved me very much, but he never could get me any work. I says, well, with friends like that, who needs enemies? It's the same thing. But I understand this word love, you know. Nothing in the world I wouldn't do for you. The result is, he does nothing. I don't need…

412.s: Hodes sued Feather for $100,000 for defamation. Feather settled for $250, costs and a subscription to Jazz Record.
412.ch: The jazz war with Leonard Feather
412.q: During that same period when I was getting smacked. Instead of taking to my fists, which I can't use very well, anyway, I found that out the hard way. I took him to -- I had a friend, a lawyer, who again I befriended the lawyer's son. And he says, sure, I'll take care of it. He told me I got a bad…

552.s: Journalism has become hype, and writers misread musicians' intentions.
552.ch: The music industry and the press
552.q: I think so. And honestly I think writers tend to write for each other. And I have seen some articles, as a matter of fact I have sort of taken a moratorium against some of the publications because I think — even some of the more popular music publications — because I have copies of articles from…

552.t: Gary Peacock, Albert Ayler and critics
552.s: The Ayler story that his music was about nothing, and composers complaining about critics.
552.ch: The music industry and the press
552.q: Yeah. I remember having a conversation about three years ago with Gary Peacock. We were both doing the Montreal Festival. And I had never met him before and I had a really fascinating conversation with him. I was very honored that he was talking to me. But he told me about an instance when he was…

553.s: On press and public response, Lateef cites Baldwin and Schopenhauer on critics misdescribing what artists do.
553.q: Well, there’s a disparity on one hand uh...frequently, during that, the earlier period. Uh one could read a review, and the critic might not even recognize the form of the music. Um...and when that happens...one can uh come to a conclusion that perhaps they really didn’t know what they were…

553.s: Down Beat polls do not matter to him, echoing Miles Davis and Schopenhauer.
553.q: No, not really. It doesn’t bother me at all. Um I go along with something that Miles [Davis] said once. He said, he said, “I’m my best critic. I don’t need anyone to tell me.”

92.t: Carter on Collins's underrated place and influence
92.s: Carter says Collins is not underrated by those who know him, agrees critics ignore him, and believes later guitarists were influenced by him.
92.ch: Gillespie and Carter on John Collins
92.q: Yeah, that's what I was telling him because I had this big stack of jazz books here while we were talking and he went through them as I had done and he's not in any of them. All he's in is Leonard's Encyclopedia and the Who's Who of Jazz by Chilton.

92.t: Known to musicians but not writers: a conspiracy?
92.s: Willard and Collins agree all musicians know him, yet critics ignore him; Willard has known his work for twenty years.
92.ch: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
92.q: I just don't understand it, whether it's a conspiracy or what. Did they get together and say look, John Collins does not exist, you know, he does not play guitar. You know.

22.t: Feud with jazz historians, the New Orleans Jazz Club and Stein
22.s: He describes a reply to a jazz-history writer, attacks Dr. Souchon and Africa-origin claims, and blames Edgar and Dave Stein for blocking his recognition.
22.q: Yes, I did. He says he's building up a new, what do you call it, on jazz. And what did I do since 1955? He don't ask me what I did before. But I took the liberty of telling him where to look for the true history on jazz and stopped writing his filthy lies. And I says, I don't have many days on this…

855.t: Fundraising letters and Hübner's criticism of the Young Tuxedo Band
855.s: Fundraising by letter had modest success; Dr. Hübner of Hamburg wrote that New Orleans birth does not guarantee good music, criticizing the Young Tuxedo recording.
855.ch: Reception in Germany and Berlin scene
855.q: Yes. Of course, I tried to do, because I originally wanted to take pictures, originally from musicians, who have been very few on plates until now. And there I had a round of writing, I spoke to all those people, from whom I believed that they were just interested in New Orleans Jazz. I also had a…

107.t: The Jazz Spotlight News article and self-doubt
107.s: His 1980 article said his music was too old fashioned; he recalls doubts about his worth, critics and writing versus playing.
107.ch: Freelance years and The Loud Minority

And there were several people behind it. One was a man named Jim Harrison, who was, he’s just been a sort of a jazz hustler all his life. He…

599.s: Quotes on his website, a 'poor man's Eddie Jefferson' review, and the power of critics.
599.q: I’ve seen a couple. One of the very first travel gigs that I ever did, I was brand new. I did a festival in Clearwater, Florida. And I was a feature. I was a quick feature in the band and it was probably like a quartet. You know, rhythm section with a saxophone and a vibraphone, and I was part of…

563.t: Hearing his first album and Floyd Levin's review
563.s: Rowe plays a track from Kellso's first released album, and they discuss a review noting Bix, Butterfield and Davison echoes, and critics generally.
563.q: That’s a good question, because there’s two cornet players on that album. It could be a little confusing. That’s the first released album that I’m on.

545.t: Musicians and critics: what journalists do and where musicians' views differ
545.s: Why musicians dislike critics, the lack of training in jazz journalism, Oscar Peterson's attack, and why musician-writers have an agenda.
545.q: Oh sure. Nobody likes to be told that their hands are dirty. That’s what criticism means. You mother is saying, “Go wash your hands again before you come to dinner.” That’s why we call it the jazz journalists instead of critics. There is really very little serious criticism that’s done in the name…

1003.t: Reviewing work he dislikes; flaws in vanity-press books
1003.s: He reviews fairly even when he dislikes something; many self-published books have spelling errors and poor binding, unlike the Joe LaBarbera and Charles Levin Bill Evans book.
1003.q: In most cases yes. I try to be fair you know. I’ll tell you something interesting, I see that more in reviewing books. Okay? And I’ll tell you why and this drives me nuts. With the proliferation of vanity presses you know anybody can publish a book if you want to spend the money on it. So you’ll…

1015.t: The Whitney Balliett 'greatest living bassist' quote
1015.s: Moore says the Balliett line was a blessing and a curse that made enemies; it was later removed from the book, though he has used it in publicity.
1015.q: Did I see it — I did one whole room in that article. Well, yeah, I did. Actually it was nice to read but it was tough to live with because I mean I didn’t agree, and it’s the kind of thing that made a lot of enemies. People I didn’t even know would come up to me and say, like I wrote it.

699.t: Critics who skip homework, and Leonard Feather on the origin of jazz polls
699.s: Critics should study and consult musicians; Leonard Feather explained how the magazine polls began, and Ridley calls them political.
699.ch: Jazz in the academy and critics
699.q: mission and I have no problem with him, that’s what he does, it’s music that you can talk over, have in the background. It’s not like when I hear Charlie Parker and I stop and say oh wow, check that out what he did going through that chord change. You know Kenny’s found his niche and hey, God bless…

934.t: Critics, record-date experts and wine analogies
934.s: He says Giddins and Japanese discographers know facts but not the music, with Jon Faddis as a wine-lore example.
934.q: A stream of consciousness. If something comes to mind I just say it. As long as Gary Giddins doesn’t hear it it’ll be fine.

701.t: The critic's function and other roles in the jazz industry
701.s: Thomas explains the critic as go-between for musicians and public, and the business jobs that support the music, which Rowe thinks are done better by musicians.
701.ch: Writing, criticism and the jazz business
701.q: But I mean there’s a function for that. There’s a critical function which basically is the go-between between the musicians and the public. Now some musicians would say we don’t need that. I mean the public, if they hear it then they can form their own impression. Well sometimes they might not hear…

220.s: Wess complains of inaccurate press, including a false post office story and a book writer's invented knife rumour.
220.q: Yeah, yeah, yeah well you’re wondering how much they listen to every day, you know? You have to listen to, and I think there’s a lot of things you shouldn’t listen to. Because you are influenced by whatever you hear, I mean whether you like it or not, you know so there’s just so many things that…

143.t: Critics, Rosenthal's hard bop book and Sweet Basil
143.s: He says writers ignored him despite his house-band run at Sweet Basil and young players coming to him.
143.q: Well, what it is, evidently, there are some people that are not too knowledgeable about what jazz really is, and when they see somebody trying to play straight-ahead, they probably say they’re not keeping up with the trends, you know. Because you take people like Jackie McLean and Tina Brooks, or…

225.t: The Esquire new-star award and views on critics and polls
225.s: His 1946 Esquire award, Andre Hodeir's untranslatable word and Johnson's balanced view of critics like Leonard Feather.
225.q: They are a breed apart from all other breeds, to say the least – critics. Obviously they are opinionated. I don’t always agree with them. I haven’t always agreed on those occasions where I was fortunate enough to win. But they have a job to do. They are paid to be opinionated. One of the strangest…

165.t: Critics who affect artists, Ralph Gleason and Peter Watrous
165.s: He accepted Ralph Gleason's criticism but tells of confronting Peter Watrous for omitting him from a Benny Carter review.
165.ch: Art Tatum, Parker and chord thinking
165.q: No, because I knew whether it was accurate or not. Ralph Gleason, whatever he said, always affected me, because I know that it was true what he said. Even when he criticized Lambert, Hendricks, and Ross for the Duke Ellington album, I accepted it. I said, “You’re right, Ralph. That’s exactly…

372.t: Konitz's objection to Ted Gioia's book on cool jazz
372.s: He feels Gioia's book ridicules the Tristano music; Kirchner disagrees.
372.ch: The Tristano group and leaving for Kenton
372.q: Okay. I wanted to mention one thing though, looking at your book recently . . . Ted Gioia, he really puts that music down.

508.t: The Cecil Taylor remark and the jazz controversy
508.s: His comment to Ken Burns that Cecil Taylor's demand for preparation was self-indulgent caused a stir among jazz writers.
508.ch: Short solos, A Love Supreme and The Tonight Show
508.q: I don’t know which episode it was, cause…when I…that’s where he put it. When he was interviewing me in my house, it wasn’t…. So…and it was in direct response to the quote that he said, you know, “People need to be ready. They need to prepare.” I said, “Man, I’m a big baseball fan. I don’t have to…

686.t: Steve Backer's apology and the critics
686.s: The Novus executive later admitted the label dropped the ball, and Marsalis discusses critics' reception of the Marsalis brothers.
686.q: There you go. [Marsalis replies.] The only redemption of – it’s a very small redemption – of RCA is that four years ago I saw Steve Backer, who was the executive producer. He saw me at a conference. He says, “Delfeayo.” Then he says, “I’m so glad I saw you.” He said, “I just wanted to tell you that…

104.t: Leonard Feather's influence as critic, producer and friend
104.s: She met Feather through Jimmy, found him generally supportive despite a bad Savoy review and the 'three strikes' remark, and recalls his ideas such as Cats vs. Chicks and Hot vs. Cool.
104.q: Oh, no. He was already established before that. I don’t know the story of Leonard’s beginnings over here. I met him through Jimmy and was at his house when he lived on Riverside Drive. He had a great apartment. I remember being there in this mob of people, feeling like just one of many people…

114.s: He says the best has yet to be heard and the polls only show what people like.
114.q: Always like to say and I've always said the best has yet to be heard. That's one of my sayings that I've always said because, you know, there are a lot of guys sitting in the corner and on the shelf in different places that can play their buns off. Guys and girls. And you don't hear them, you know.…

565.s: He talks about critics, Lawrence Gilman, and Elgar.
565.ch: Charlie, critics and the Latin Jazz Grammy
565.q: watch out til you get your spinal volt... Charlie, after 50 years old you don’t get blood into your disk, Charlie so you need the spinal volt.” And whatever I told him, he used to go, “Oh my God!” [LAUGHS] My only thing was, with all the troubles that I had, the only thing that you can do for…

68.t: Critics: George Frazier's review of his first Basie nights
68.s: Critic George Frazier at the Southland in Boston turns out to praise Tate as Herschel Evans's replacement.
68.q: Well, I've never been mad with any, I really haven't. I've been -- critics have been pretty nice to me, really. I haven't had -- ever had one to really put me down. I'll tell you, when I first joined the band once, I thought one was going to put me down. His name was George Frazier He used to be up…

166.t: Feather's revenge in Metronome and losing the Esquire award
166.s: Feather panned records he was on; the award went to Oscar Pettiford.
166.q: So Leonard and I we didn't speak anymore from then on. Cause all of the, like they had a thing in the Downbeat, the Three Deuces. He and George Simon and Barry Ulanov (Phonetic). They reviewed all records and the star ratings, you know, how many.

383.t: Critics as parasites: George Frazier and the Tilton insult
383.s: Wilson says Frazier made his name by calling Goodman's singer Martha Tilton bad, then left jazz writing.
383.ch: Opinions on pop music, jazz education and the business
383.q: George Frazier busted into the jazz world years ago and created a big niche for himself by coming out in some important jazz publication by saying Martha Tilton stinks. When Benny Goodman was on top, after the '38 concert, with Nancy Tilton singing, and here's an unknown writer coming up saying…

454.t: What a critic should be, and the danger of Times reviews
454.s: Critics should report what happened and review last; one reviewer can kill a play.
454.ch: Second interview: bass, Parker and Miles
454.q: That's a hard thing to say, because to me, I don't go to Broadway plays like I used to. But critics are supposed to write what is seen, in the case of -- for instance, I remember John Wilson reviewed a concert of mine. If he goes to a Beatle concert, he tells you there were millions of people…

96.t: George Frazier's 1941 Down Beat review of the band at Nick's
96.s: Johnston reads Frazier's praise of McPartland's band at Nick's.
96.q: I think that goes the same for any band really. And I'm glad that he wrote that because you don't always play well. You can't always play well. I assure you of that.

171.t: McShann underrated; Earl Hines the same
171.s: McShann is introduced only as Parker's discoverer, and Hines too is asked mainly about others.
171.ch: Meeting Jay McShann and Martin's on the Plaza
171.q: Yeah. We were talking about that, too. It kind of hurts him, but he doesn't let that show, you know. He mentioned one time, he said that, "everybody's introducing me as the man who just up and discovered Charlie Parker."
